title: Catalog assurance narrative playbook
content:
Purpose:

This playbook captures the recommended positioning, core claims, and tactical messaging for the Model Catalog product area focused on open models and 'Verified Profiles'. It's intended for PMs, growth, content, and sales enablement to create consistent, testable copy across docs, web, and demos.

Audience and use cases:
- Engineering-first buyers evaluating open model options for production inference (latency/cost-sensitive SaaS teams).
- Platform and SRE teams assessing model governance and rollout risk.
- Solutions engineers and AEs preparing buyer-facing comparisons and POCs.

High level positioning thesis (one sentence):
"A model catalog that removes guesswork — clear, empirical profiles for open models so teams can pick a model by measured tradeoffs (quality, cost, latency, safety) and push to production with confidence."

Core messaging pillars (rank-ordered):
1) Empirical clarity: standardized, repeatable evals and runtime profiles that surface the real-world tradeoffs of open models.
2) Trust-by-transparency: provenance, tuning lineage, and dataset/benchmark footprints in each Verified Profile.
3) Production-readiness: runtime metrics (token latency, memory footprint, quantization compatibility) + rollout controls so customers can predict costs and avoid regressions.
4) Guardrails & safety signal: scoring for hallucination risk, safety filters, and recommended mitigations.
5) Choice with guidance: curated recommendations (by workload type) that guide non-expert buyers to good defaults.

Unique proof points to emphasize:
- Unified evaluation harness: same prompt sets, same infra, same metrics across all catalog models — removes apples-to-oranges comparisons.
- Runtime-first profiles: we report end-to-end median/95th token latency on N1 sequence distributions, not just FLOPs or model size.
- Verified lineage: every profile contains clear notes on the base model, instruction-tuning data (if any), quantization steps, and known license constraints.
- Quality monitoring: integrated continuous evals so customers are alerted to regressions after a model update or a quantized deploy.

Competitive differentiation notes (short-form):
- Versus managed LLM APIs: those sell consistency & simplicity; we trade on transparency and cost control for teams that want to optimize inference economics without blindboxes.
- Versus self-host runtimes: pure runtimes often leave the burden of model choice & evaluation to the customer; our catalog pairs runtime profiles and curated recommendations, reducing time-to-safe-serve.
- Versus open-model marketplaces: marketplaces list models; our Verified Profiles add operational signals plus continuous quality monitoring tied to rolling releases and rollback policies.

Customer pain statements (language for landing pages / emails):
- "Which open model will give us the same accuracy but half the inference bill?"
- "We need repeatable tests — not vendor slides — to validate a model for customer data."
- "Our team can’t afford a model update to silently worsen prompt quality in production."

Primary claims and supporting evidence (for sales decks):
- Claim: "Pick models by measured tradeoffs." Evidence: public benchmark matrix + customer POC that reduced per-token cost 35% while meeting response quality thresholds. (link to POC deck).
- Claim: "Ship with confidence." Evidence: rollout logs showing automatic canary rollback after quality drop on a Held-out prompt set.
- Claim: "Understand safety risk." Evidence: hallucination-score distributions and recommended mitigations per model.

Objections and counterpoints (AE rebuttal bullets):
- Objection: "Open models are risky — we need enterprise-grade guarantees."
  Rebuttal: "Verified Profiles show safety and calibration signals, and Redwood can enforce policy via private deployments + rollout guardrails and SLA-backed Dedicated capacity."
- Objection: "We already benchmark ourselves."
  Rebuttal: "Great — bring your tests. We ingest customer prompt sets and run them in the same harness; the difference is we ship the runtime-level latency/cost profile as part of the outcome so you can predict ops impact."

Label semantics: What 'Verified Profile' means exactly (internal definition):
- Standardized: tests run on Redwood infra with documented parameters.
- Provenance: upstream model name/hash, training/tuning notes, license statement.
- Runtime metrics: per-token latency median/95th, seq-length scaling, GPU & CPU footprint estimates.
- Quality signals: task-specific F1/EM where relevant, instruction-following score, hallucination rate on curated dataset.
- Safety & compliance notes: any known biases, red-team notes, recommended filters.
- Change log: model version history and what changed between builds.

Content formats and examples to produce (requested assets):
- One-pager 'How to read a Verified Profile' (visual) for product pages.
- Short explainer video script (90s) for onboarding flows.
- Competitor comparison table for AE battlecards.
- Two landing page hero variants: 'Predictable inference economics' and 'Production-grade model choice'.

Suggested hero copy options (test both):
- Option A: "Open models, explained — pick the best model for your product by real metrics, not guesswork."
- Option B: "Verified profiles for open models — production signals, safety context, and cost numbers you can act on."

Recommended microcopy for profile page (quick scan panels):
- "Latency & cost — measured on Redwood serving runtime with example sequence distributions."
- "Quality snapshot — instruction-following and hallucination rates on standard and customer-held prompts."
- "Provenance & lineage — who published the model, how it was tuned, and license constraints."

Go-to-market tactics and experiments (first 90 days):
1) AE enablement sprint: 3 battlecards covering retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), summarization, and code-assist use-cases; include recommended model picks and expected cost/latency tradeoffs.
2) Microsite MVP: a sortable, filterable model table with Verified Profile badges and a CTA for a 'compatibility POC'.
3) Proof packs for pilots: packaged test suites + expected SLOs for customers to run in a 2-week POC.
4) Webinar w/ SRE customer: "How we shaved 30% off inference bills with model selection and quantization."

Metrics to track (initial success criteria):
- % of hosted API requests using catalog-recommended model variants.
- POC-to-paid conversion rate when a Verified Profile is included in the proposal.
- Reduction in average cost-per-response for pilot customers who follow catalog guidance.

Open questions & risks (to resolve in product):
- How often to re-run the full harness on large model updates — monthly? on commit? balance cost vs staleness.
- Legal: how to display license/usage restrictions without exposing legal risk. Need legal-approved phrasing.
- Signal noise: hallucination scoring is brittle — require multi-metric syntheses rather than raw rates.

Next steps / owner actions:
- PM: finalize Verified Profile schema (Jordan) — due 2025-02-05.
- SWE: prototype the public model table with sort/filter by latency/cost/quality (Rafael) — demo by 2025-02-20.
- Content: draft 'How to read a Verified Profile' one-pager (Maya) — first draft 2025-01-30.

Appendix: quick competitive notes (raw):
- Vendor A (managed API): sells convenience; lacks transparency into what instruction-tuning or quant steps were applied. Opportunity: position transparency + rollout safety.
- Vendor B (self-host runtime): strong on throughput; catalog suffers from lack of standardized evals — opportunity: offer shared harness and profile portability.
- Open marketplace X: many models but low operational signals; Verified Profile badge can become a trust signal across ecosystems.

Draft marketing email subject lines to A/B test:
- "Which open model will save your team 20–40% on inference?"
- "Meet Verified Profiles: real model numbers, not marketing slides"
- "Ship models with confidence — see runtime-backed profiles"

Notes to content team: keep examples concrete (expected ms/token, sample prompts, and a short table of quality tradeoffs). Avoid grandiose claims about "best" — focus on measured tradeoffs and reproducible results.

Links / artifacts referenced: CONFLUENCE-2389 (Eval harness design), JIRA-MLCAT-42 (Verified Profile schema), github.com/redwood-inference/model-catalog/PR-88 (initial profile UI).

Unresolved edits: still debating whether 'Verified' should be a gated process (manual review) or automatic badge with thresholds; both have tradeoffs for velocity vs trust.

Author notes: this doc is intentionally pragmatic — it's a playbook for quick, testable messaging and field collateral rather than finalized brand copy. Expect iterations after the first customer pilots.
